q: A reversible reaction in a closed vessel is at chemical equilibrium when:
o: The concentrations of reactants and products become equal
The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
Both the forward and the reverse reactions stop
All the reactants have been converted into products
x: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations then stay constant, but they are usually not equal to each other.

q: The Kc expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is:
o: [N₂][H₂]³ / [NH₃]²
[NH₃] / [N₂][H₂]
[NH₃]² / [N₂][H₂]³
2[NH₃] / [N₂] 3[H₂]
x: Kc is products over reactants, each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Coefficients become powers, not multipliers.

q: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in conditions, the system:
o: Stops reacting until the change is removed
Always shifts towards the products
Shifts its equilibrium position so as to partly undo the change
Changes its Kc to match the new conditions
x: The equilibrium moves in the direction that opposes the applied change, such as using up added reactant or absorbing added heat. It does not always favour products.

q: In the Haber process, ammonia is manufactured by the reaction of:
o: Nitrogen and oxygen
Hydrogen and nitric acid
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Nitrogen monoxide and water
x: The Haber process combines nitrogen and hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The forward reaction is exothermic.

q: Which statement about the concentrations in a mixture at chemical equilibrium is correct?
o: They are always equal for reactants and products
They remain constant with time but are usually not equal to each other
They keep rising for products and falling for reactants
They change continuously in a regular cycle
x: At equilibrium the amounts no longer change because both reactions run at the same rate. Constant does not mean equal: the ratio is fixed by Kc.

q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium constant Kc is:
o: [SO₃]² / [SO₂]²[O₂]
[SO₂]²[O₂] / [SO₃]²
[SO₃] / [SO₂][O₂]
[SO₃]² / [SO₂][O₂]²
x: SO₃ is the product with coefficient 2; SO₂ has coefficient 2 and O₂ has 1. So Kc = [SO₃]² / [SO₂]²[O₂]. The inverted expression would be Kc for the reverse reaction.

q: More N₂ is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at constant temperature and volume. What happens?
o: The equilibrium shifts to the left and NH₃ decomposes
The equilibrium does not change
The value of Kc increases
The equilibrium shifts to the right and more NH₃ forms
x: Adding a reactant is opposed by using it up, so the forward reaction is favoured and more NH₃ forms. Kc is unchanged because the temperature is constant.

q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is:
o: Vanadium(V) oxide
Platinum gauze
Finely divided nickel
Finely divided iron
x: Iron (with promoters) catalyses ammonia synthesis. V₂O₅ is used in the Contact process for SO₃ and nickel in hydrogenation of oils.

q: A state of chemical equilibrium can be set up only when a reversible reaction is carried out:
o: In a closed system, so that no substance escapes
In an open beaker, so that gases can leave
Only in the presence of a catalyst
Only at a very high temperature
x: Products must stay in contact with each other to react back, so a closed system is needed. A catalyst only speeds up the approach to equilibrium; it is not required for it.

q: For which equilibrium does Kc have no units?
o: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
x: Kc has no units when the total moles in the expression are the same on both sides. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI there are 2 on each side, so the units cancel.

q: In the reversible reaction CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, the water formed is removed continuously. The effect is that:
o: Less ester is formed, because the equilibrium shifts to the left
The reaction stops
The equilibrium constant becomes zero
More ester is formed, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
x: Removing a product is opposed by forming more of it, so the forward reaction is favoured and the yield of ester rises.

q: The temperature used in the Haber process is about:
x: A moderate temperature of roughly 400–500 °C is used. Lower temperatures make the reaction too slow, and much higher ones give a very poor yield.

q: Which of the following reactions is treated as irreversible, i.e. it goes practically to completion?
o: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI in a closed flask
N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ in a sealed tube
PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ in a closed vessel
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (burning of methane)
x: Combustion of methane goes to completion and the products do not re-form methane and oxygen. The other three are standard textbook examples of reversible reactions that reach equilibrium.

q: What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
o: mol⁻² dm⁶
mol² dm⁻⁶
mol dm⁻³
No units
x: Kc = [NH₃]²/[N₂][H₂]³ has units (mol dm⁻³)² / (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻², which is mol⁻² dm⁶.

q: The pressure on the equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is increased at constant temperature. The equilibrium shifts:
o: To the right, because more gas molecules are on that side
To the right, because Kc increases with pressure
Neither way, because pressure never affects equilibrium
To the left, because fewer gas molecules are on that side
x: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. There is 1 mol on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the equilibrium moves to the left.

q: The pressure used in the Haber process is about:
o: 1 atm
5 atm
5000 atm
x: A high pressure of about 200–300 atm is used to favour ammonia. Much higher pressures would need very costly, strong equipment.

q: Chemical equilibrium is described as dynamic because:
o: The reaction stops once the products are formed
The concentrations of all substances keep changing
The temperature of the mixture keeps changing
The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates
x: At equilibrium the reactions have not stopped; molecules keep reacting in both directions at the same rate, so there is no net change in composition.

q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1 and [HI] = 0.8 mol dm⁻³. What is Kc?
x: Kc = [HI]² / [H₂][I₂] = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. Forgetting to square [HI] gives 80, and inverting the expression gives about 0.0156.

q: A change in pressure has no effect on the position of which equilibrium?
o: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
x: Pressure only matters when the number of gas moles differs on the two sides. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has 2 mol of gas on each side.

q: High pressure increases the yield of ammonia in the Haber process because:
o: The forward reaction is endothermic
High pressure increases the value of Kc
4 moles of gaseous reactants form only 2 moles of gaseous product
High pressure makes the iron catalyst more active
x: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ goes from 4 mol of gas to 2 mol. By Le Chatelier's principle, high pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.

q: A little radioactive iodine, as I₂, is added to an equilibrium mixture of H₂(g), I₂(g) and HI(g) at constant temperature. After some time, the radioactivity is found:
o: In both I₂ and HI, showing that the forward and reverse reactions are still going on
Only in I₂, because the reactions stop once equilibrium is reached
Only in HI, because all the added I₂ reacts
In I₂ only at first and then nowhere, because it decays at once
x: At equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates, so labelled I₂ forms labelled HI and labelled HI breaks down again, spreading radioactivity into both. Concentrations stay constant only because the rates are equal, not because the reactions have stopped; that misconception gives 'only in I₂'.

q: At the same temperature, flask X starts with 1.0 mol H₂ and 1.0 mol I₂, and flask Y of the same volume starts with 2.0 mol HI. When both have reached equilibrium (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI):
o: Flask X contains more HI than flask Y
Flask Y contains more HI than flask X
Both flasks contain the same amounts of H₂, I₂ and HI
Flask Y contains no H₂ or I₂, because HI is the product
x: Both flasks hold the same total of 2 mol H atoms and 2 mol I atoms in the same volume at the same temperature, so they reach the same equilibrium mixture: equilibrium can be approached from either side. Thinking of HI only as a product leads to the last option.

q: Only X is placed in a closed vessel and the reversible reaction X ⇌ Y begins. Until equilibrium is reached:
o: Both rates rise until they become equal
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they become equal
The forward rate stays constant while the reverse rate rises
The forward rate falls to zero and the reverse rate rises to its maximum
x: As X is used up its concentration falls, so the forward rate falls; as Y builds up, the reverse rate rises. Equilibrium is reached when the two rates are equal, not when either becomes zero.

q: Which is an example of a physical dynamic equilibrium rather than a chemical one?
o: Water and its vapour in a sealed flask at constant temperature
N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) in a sealed tube
Ethanoic acid ionising in water
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) in a closed vessel
x: In the sealed flask, evaporation and condensation go on at equal rates with no new substance formed: a physical equilibrium. The other three make or break chemical bonds, so they are chemical equilibria. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is often mistaken for a change of state because both are gases.

q: For the one-step reversible reaction X ⇌ Y, the forward rate constant is 4.0 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ and the reverse rate constant is 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. At equilibrium, what is the ratio [Y]/[X]?
x: At equilibrium the rates are equal: kf[X] = kr[Y], so [Y]/[X] = kf/kr = (4.0 × 10⁻²)/(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 20, which is Kc. Dividing the other way gives 0.05; multiplying the constants gives 8.0 × 10⁻⁵.

q: 1.0 mol of PCl₅ is heated in a closed 1.0 dm³ vessel: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). At equilibrium 0.50 mol of Cl₂ is present. What is Kc at this temperature?
o: 0.25 mol dm⁻³
1.0 mol dm⁻³
2.0 mol dm⁻³
0.50 mol dm⁻³
x: Forming 0.50 mol Cl₂ also forms 0.50 mol PCl₃ and uses 0.50 mol PCl₅, leaving 0.50 mol. Kc = [PCl₃][Cl₂]/[PCl₅] = (0.50 × 0.50)/0.50 = 0.50 mol dm⁻³. Using the initial 1.0 mol for PCl₅ gives 0.25; inverting the expression gives 2.0.

q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the relation between Kp and Kc is:
o: Kp = Kc(RT)
Kp = Kc(RT)²
Kp = Kc
Kp = Kc(RT)⁻¹
x: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = gas moles of products − gas moles of reactants = 2 − 3 = −1, so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻¹. Taking reactants minus products gives Δn = +1 and the wrong sign of the power.

q: At a certain temperature the numerical value of Kc is 0.50 for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). What is the numerical value of Kc at the same temperature for NH₃(g) ⇌ ½N₂(g) + 1.5H₂(g)?
x: Reversing an equation inverts K: 1/0.50 = 2.0. Halving all coefficients takes the square root: √2.0 ≈ 1.41. Stopping after reversing gives 2.0; taking the square root of 0.50 without reversing gives 0.71.

q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kc = 50 at a certain temperature. A mixture at this temperature has [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and [HI] = 0.50 mol dm⁻³. What happens next?
o: The forward reaction is faster, so more HI forms until the quotient equals Kc
The reverse reaction is faster, so HI decomposes
The mixture is already at equilibrium
Nothing can be predicted without the value of Kp
x: Reaction quotient Q = [HI]²/[H₂][I₂] = 0.25/0.010 = 25, which is less than Kc = 50, so the mixture moves forward, making more HI. Forgetting to square [HI] gives 0.50/0.010 = 50 and the false conclusion that it is already at equilibrium.

q: At equilibrium in N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at a certain temperature, the partial pressures are p(NO₂) = 0.40 atm and p(N₂O₄) = 0.80 atm. What is Kp?
o: 0.50 atm
0.20 atm
2.0 atm
5.0 atm
x: Kp = p(NO₂)²/p(N₂O₄) = (0.40)²/0.80 = 0.16/0.80 = 0.20 atm. Not squaring p(NO₂) gives 0.50; inverting the squared expression gives 5.0.

q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −197 kJ mol⁻¹. If the temperature of the equilibrium mixture is raised, what happens?
o: The equilibrium shifts to the left but Kc stays the same
The equilibrium shifts to the right and Kc increases
The equilibrium shifts to the left and Kc decreases
The equilibrium does not shift; only the rates increase
x: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, here the reverse reaction, so less SO₃ is present. Unlike changes in concentration or pressure, a temperature change alters the value of K itself: for an exothermic reaction Kc falls. Thinking K never changes gives the second option.

q: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction that is already at equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
o: Only the forward rate increases, so more product forms
Kc increases because the activation energy is lowered
The forward and reverse rates increase equally, so the composition and Kc do not change
The equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles
x: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions by the same amount, so both rates rise equally; it only helps a system reach equilibrium sooner. The yield and Kc are unchanged. Believing a catalyst speeds up only the forward reaction gives the second option.

q: Argon is pumped into an equilibrium mixture of N₂(g), H₂(g) and NH₃(g) at constant volume and temperature, so the total pressure rises. What happens to the amount of NH₃?
o: It stays the same, because the partial pressures of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ do not change
It increases, because the total pressure has increased
It decreases, because argon dilutes the reactants
It increases, because argon acts as a catalyst
x: At constant volume, the amounts and concentrations (and so the partial pressures) of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ are unchanged by adding an unreactive gas, so the reaction quotient still equals K and nothing shifts. Applying 'higher pressure favours fewer moles' to the total pressure gives the tempting wrong answer.

q: N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹. Which change increases the equilibrium amount of NO?
o: Raising the pressure
Raising the temperature
Adding a catalyst
Lowering the temperature
x: The forward reaction is endothermic, so a higher temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so pressure has no effect, and a catalyst does not change the position. Lowering the temperature would favour the exothermic reverse reaction.

q: In water, yellow chromate and orange dichromate ions are in equilibrium: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O. A few drops of NaOH solution are added to an orange solution. The colour:
o: Becomes deeper orange, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
Turns yellow, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the equilibrium shifts to the left
Does not change, because Na⁺ and OH⁻ do not appear in the equation
Turns green, because chromium is reduced
x: OH⁻ neutralises H⁺, lowering its concentration; the equilibrium shifts to the left to replace H⁺, converting orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ into yellow CrO₄²⁻. A substance not in the equation can still act by removing one that is, which is why the 'no change' option is wrong.

q: The catalyst used for the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ in the contact process is:
o: Finely divided iron
Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅
Nickel
Manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂
x: The contact process uses V₂O₅ at about 450 °C. Finely divided iron is the catalyst of the Haber process, nickel is used for hydrogenating oils, and MnO₂ catalyses the decomposition of H₂O₂; mixing up the Haber and contact catalysts is the usual slip.

q: In the contact process, SO₃ is absorbed in 98% H₂SO₄ to form oleum, H₂S₂O₇, instead of being passed directly into water. The reason is that SO₃ and water:
o: Do not react with each other at all
React to form H₂SO₃ instead of H₂SO₄
Form an explosive mixture
React so exothermically that a fine mist of acid forms, which is hard to condense
x: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ releases so much heat that the acid forms as a mist that escapes absorption. Absorbing SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ gives oleum, which is then diluted with water to the required strength. SO₃ certainly reacts with water, and H₂SO₃ comes from SO₂, not SO₃.

q: In the Haber process the forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia. A temperature of about 450 °C is still used because:
o: Ammonia cannot exist as a gas below 450 °C
The equilibrium yield of ammonia increases with temperature
Nitrogen and hydrogen form a different product below 450 °C
At low temperature the reaction is too slow, so 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield
x: A lower temperature favours ammonia at equilibrium, but the rate becomes far too slow even with the catalyst; about 450 °C gives an acceptable yield quickly. The yield actually falls as temperature rises, so the third option reverses Le Chatelier's principle.

q: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) has fewer moles of gas on the right, yet the contact process runs at only about 1–2 atm. The main reason is that:
o: Conversion to SO₃ is already very high at this pressure, so the extra cost of high pressure is not justified
Pressure has no effect on this equilibrium
High pressure would shift the equilibrium to the left
The V₂O₅ catalyst works only at exactly 1 atm
x: High pressure would favour SO₃ (3 mol gas → 2 mol), but with excess air and the catalyst the conversion is already about 98–99% near atmospheric pressure, so expensive high-pressure plant is not worth it. Saying pressure has no effect ignores the change in gas moles.

q: In a Haber reactor, 28 g of N₂ is mixed with 12 g of H₂, and 15% of the nitrogen is converted to ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. What mass of NH₃ is formed?
x: 28 g N₂ = 1.0 mol; 12 g H₂ = 6.0 mol, more than the 3.0 mol needed, so N₂ is limiting. 15% of 1.0 mol = 0.15 mol N₂ gives 0.30 mol NH₃ = 0.30 × 17 = 5.1 g. Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio gives 2.55 ≈ 2.6 g; 34 g ignores the 15%; basing it on H₂ gives 10.2 g.
